title: Lessons From 9/11 and Its Aftermath | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: CFR president Michael Froman's twenty-fifth-anniversary reflection argues the United States won the battle but lost the war after 9/11 by overextending into Iraq and Afghanistan, opening space for China's rise and Russia's belligerence while eroding domestic trust in institutions. He draws three forward lessons: threat diversification including domestic terrorism, frontier-technology diffusion as a new attack surface, and institutional redesign of the domestic security apparatus.

themes.theme: Strategic overextension as the core post-9/11 error

insights.claim: The twenty-year US campaign that began with removing the Taliban ended with the Taliban's return, a case of winning the battle but effectively losing the war because the United States overextended itself.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Overextension, not capability, was the binding failure; a template for judging current open-ended US commitments.
insights.quote: We won the battle but effectively lost the war, in part because we overextended ourselves.
insights.locator: What began with the successful removal of the Taliban

insights.claim: The invasion of Iraq was justified with poor intelligence amid post-9/11 fear and anxiety, and set the United States on a depleting, destructive and distracting path.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Decision-making under acute fear degrades intelligence standards; a recurring risk premium around post-shock policy responses.
insights.quote: The invasion of Iraq, justified with poor intelligence amid the fear and anxiety felt in the wake of 9/11
insights.locator: The invasion of Iraq, justified with poor intelligence

insights.claim: Two 'forever' wars created an opening for rising or resurgent powers to realign the global balance of power, and the world is still living with the long tail of that shift.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Frames today's multipolarity as partly self-inflicted; implies the US cannot simply reverse it by re-engaging.
insights.quote: the long tail of which we are living with today

insights.claim: Today's balance-of-power shift has multiple causes beyond 9/11, including China's rise, Russia's belligerence, the global financial crisis, Brexit, COVID-19, and Trump's questioning of how the US engages with the world.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Guards against single-cause narratives when modeling geopolitical regime change; several independent drivers must be tracked.
insights.locator: The complex shifts in the balance of power in the twenty-first century

insights.claim: The Department of Homeland Security, the Patriot Act, and intelligence community expansion made the United States safer from foreign threats but coincided with more acrimonious, less trusting politics and a loss of faith in government, the press, and civil society.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Security gains were purchased with institutional trust, an erosion that now constrains US policy capacity at home.
insights.quote: But our politics became more acrimonious and less trusting
insights.locator: The establishment of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

insights.claim: Because a far smaller share of the population saw combat than in World War II and most Americans returned to normal life quickly, that normalcy calcified into acceptance of a grinding war and made the 'forever' quality of the forever wars possible.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Low domestic cost-sharing is what allows open-ended conflicts to persist; watch for the same structure in current commitments.
insights.quote: The normalcy that returned after 9/11 soon calcified into an acceptance of a grinding war
insights.locator: However much 9/11 remade the country in profound ways

insights.claim: Post-Pearl Harbor America mobilized the entire country, drafting hundreds of thousands, retooling factories and converting to a wartime economy, whereas post-9/11 America did not, making the two shocks structurally incomparable despite the common framing.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Analogies to Pearl Harbor mislead on the economic channel: a national security shock need not imply industrial mobilization or a wartime economy.
insights.quote: It changed the everyday lives of every person.
insights.locator: After Pearl Harbor, the entire country was mobilized

insights.claim: On the eve of the 9/11 attacks the United States was enjoying an economic and geopolitical peace dividend, as the lone superpower left uncontested and thus unrestrained by the Soviet Union's fall.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Marks the peak of the unipolar peace dividend, a baseline against which today's defense and security spending burden should be measured.
insights.locator: On the eve of the attacks, the United States was enjoying its peace dividend

themes.theme: Forward-looking lessons: threat diversification, technology, institutions

insights.claim: Four former secretaries of homeland security agreed that achieving security at home now requires addressing the diversification of threats, including domestic and political terrorism.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Signals bipartisan elite consensus that the threat center of gravity has moved inside US borders, shifting where security budgets go.
insights.locator: As all the secretaries noted, achieving security at home

insights.claim: 9/11 was a technological revolution in which weaponizing passenger planes was a shocking innovation few could reasonably have foreseen, and today's faster technological progress plus diffusion of access to the frontier creates a new set of comparable threats.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Frontier-technology diffusion is explicitly framed as a security threat vector, which supports tighter controls on access to advanced capabilities.
insights.quote: The notion of weaponizing passenger planes was a shocking innovation that few could reasonably have seen coming.
insights.locator: Second, it is important to remember that 9/11 also marked a technological revolution

insights.claim: Drone technology and new cyber capabilities represent a sea change in the nature of war that 9/11 set in motion, according to former Acting CIA Director John McLaughlin.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Drone and cyber capability are named as the durable structural shift in warfare, a persistent demand driver for those defense segments.
insights.locator: With 9/11 also came a sea change in the nature of war

insights.claim: Poorly structured government institutions made it difficult if not impossible to share crucial intelligence about the al-Qaeda threat before 9/11, and DHS was established too late because it was needed on September 10.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Institutional design, not information scarcity, was the failure point; a lens for judging whether current agencies are structured for today's threats.
insights.quote: DHS was established too late—it was needed on September 10.

insights.claim: Former DHS Secretary Jeh Johnson's proposal for an entirely overhauled domestic security apparatus is held up as the kind of proactive institutional thinking the moment requires.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: A named reform proposal worth tracking as a possible template if US domestic security architecture is restructured.
insights.locator: Former DHS Secretary Jeh Johnson’s proposal

insights.claim: The United States cannot afford complacency about the shifting balance of power, evolving threats, and the government structure, tools and technology needed for national security at this critical moment.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: The head of CFR framing the present as a critical inflection point is itself a signal about elite risk perception.
insights.quote: We cannot afford complacency—particularly at this critical moment in history
insights.locator: One thing is clear: We cannot afford complacency
